question: In a catalogue of every star bright enough to detect, the farther stars are, on average, intrinsically brighter. Why?
options: Bright stars gather far from the Sun
Only luminous stars are seen that far
Nearby stars are younger and fainter
answer: Only luminous stars are seen that far. Close to the Sun a catalogue picks up faint and bright stars alike; far away, only the brightest clear the limit. Gunnar Malmquist described this bias in the 1920s. Assume a typical brightness for a distant star in such a catalogue and it lands too close.
move: Far away only the loudest are heard, so average them with care.
ask: Which sample I rely on is made only of the loudest, most extreme members?
trap: Taking a pattern in the catalogue as a pattern in the sky.
reference: Binney & Merrifield, Galactic Astronomy, Princeton University Press, 1998
